chunks.label: NASA: Counteracting Bone and Muscle Loss in Microgravity
chunks.text: In space, astronauts' weight-bearing bones become roughly 1% less dense for every month. Bone-building cells slow down while the cells that break down old or damaged bone keep working at their normal pace. Muscles weaken because they no longer need to work as hard. Crews exercise an average of about two hours a day, using treadmills, stationary bicycles and the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED), which simulates weightlifting. Pre-flight exercise training improves performance on station. Researchers found decreased expression of genes related to muscle growth and metabolism in microgravity, and drugs such as myostatin inhibitors may help prevent bone and muscle loss.

chunks.label: NASA: Astronaut Exercise
chunks.text: Astronauts on the space station average two hours of exercise per day to maintain bone and muscle health. Equipment includes ARED (a piston and flywheel system that mimics weightlifting in weightlessness), the T2 treadmill and CEVIS, a computer-controlled cycle ergometer with vibration isolation. Without Earth's gravity both bone and muscle atrophy, becoming smaller and weaker. Early programmes of long, low-intensity workouts proved ineffective; high-intensity, low-volume exercise was found more effective, which also saves crew time and equipment wear.

chunks.label: NASA: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
chunks.text: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) is a set of eye and brain changes linked to weightlessness. Chronic weightlessness can shift blood and cerebrospinal fluid toward the head, which can lead to optic nerve swelling, folds in the retina, flattening of the back of the eye and swelling in the brain. Approximately 70 percent of astronauts aboard the International Space Station experience some swelling in the back of their eyes. Some astronauts have only mild changes; others have clinically significant outcomes. The risk is higher on longer missions. The long-term health outcome is unknown and actively being investigated. NASA is investigating nutritional supplements that could protect the eyes and mechanical interventions that may help reverse headward fluid shifts. AstroDocX does not yet include vision or SANS self-tests; they are on its roadmap.

chunks.label: NASA HRP: Space Radiation hazard
chunks.text: NASA considers space radiation one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight. The sources are high-energy galactic cosmic rays, which are remnants of supernovas, and solar storms such as solar particle events and coronal mass ejections. Radiation exposure increases cancer risk, damages the central nervous system, can alter cognitive function, reduce motor function and prompt behavioral changes. Astronauts cannot see or feel it. NASA scientists are studying its effects on the human body and developing ways to monitor and protect against it.

chunks.label: NASA HRP: Isolation and Confinement hazard
chunks.text: Behavioral responses occur among groups of people far from Earth who are isolated and confined in a small space over a long period. Sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload compound this and may lead to decreased performance, adverse health outcomes and compromised mission objectives. NASA's Human Research Program studies behavioral health monitoring, workload and performance, circadian rhythm management and team dynamics. Countermeasures include careful crew selection, training and support, journaling tools, and analog missions in habitats such as HERA and CHAPEA that simulate confinement.

chunks.label: NTRS 20160004365: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders
chunks.text: NASA's evidence report says the average incidence of an adverse behavioral health event during a space mission is relatively low under current conditions, but that the likelihood of an adverse cognitive or behavioral condition or psychiatric disorder greatly increases with mission length. Mood and anxiety disturbances have occurred historically, with no severe behavioral emergencies documented on missions to date. Even when they do not threaten the mission, such conditions adversely affect individual and crew health, welfare and performance, so prevention, early detection and treatment countermeasures are essential.

chunks.label: NTRS 20160003864: Risk of Performance Decrements from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload
chunks.text: NASA's evidence report states that astronauts consistently average less sleep during spaceflight than on the ground. Ground evidence indicates the amount of sleep astronauts get is likely to lead to performance impairment and short- and long-term health consequences. The causes of the sleep loss remain unknown, and the report calls for tools to measure individual sleep needs. It also flags sleep inertia: ground studies show it takes two to four hours to reach optimal performance after waking from a sleep episode, a hazard when crews must respond quickly to an emergency.

chunks.label: NTRS 20160012725: CO2 levels, congestion and headaches on the ISS
chunks.text: A NASA analysis of International Space Station expeditions 2 to 31 found that for each 1 mmHg increase in CO2, the odds of a crew member reporting congestion doubled, and that congestion emerges at roughly 1 mmHg lower than headache reports. To keep the chance of congestion below 1 percent, the average 7-day CO2 level would need to stay under 1.5 mmHg. The study confirmed earlier findings linking CO2 to headaches.

chunks.label: NASA: Landmark Twins Study Reveals Resilience of Human Body in Space
chunks.text: In NASA's Twins Study, astronaut Scott Kelly spent nearly a year on the space station while his identical twin stayed on Earth. The flu vaccine given in space worked as it does on Earth, so the immune system responded properly. Scott's telomere length unexpectedly increased in space and shortened after he returned, going back to normal within six months; his twin's stayed stable. Most gene-expression changes normalized within six months of return, but a small percentage of genes related to the immune system and DNA repair did not return to baseline. The study also found changes in cognitive function and vision-related changes. Most physiological changes reversed within six months back on Earth.

chunks.label: NASA HRP: The five hazards of human spaceflight
chunks.text: NASA's Human Research Program groups spaceflight risk into five hazards. Gravity Fields: astronauts' entire bodies, including muscles, bones, inner ear and organs, must adjust to the new gravities they encounter. Distance from Earth: instructions, new supplies and medical care become increasingly challenging to receive from Earth. Hostile/Closed Environments: maintaining a safe ecosystem inside a spacecraft presents unique challenges, including temperature, pressure and microbial monitoring. Space Radiation and Isolation and Confinement are the other two.
